description: Beyond Cloud transforms NASA and Earth data into stories. Our mission: go beyond the data, find the story, share the impact. Join us to turn science into meaningful narratives.
summary: Abandoned but not Forgotten is an interactive web museum that tells the stories of the machines NASA left behind on the Moon, on Mars, and in deep space. Visitors enter a cinematic landing page, then follow a 12-scene story narrated in a human voice. In it, machines such as the Apollo 11 lander, Surveyor 3, Spirit, Opportunity, and Ingenuity speak in the first person. A Ghost Hardware Map lets them tap glowing dots on the Moon and Mars to hear how each machine worked, what it found, and how its story ended. An archive of 13 missions adds photos, key details, eight technical specs, and a quiz for each mission at three reading levels (ages 0-5, 6-10, and 11-16).
details:
How I address the challenge:
School-age students mostly hear about active missions. This project turns the histories of dormant hardware into narrative. It shows how each machine operated and ties the engineering to the science it made possible:

  • Surveyor 3 showed the Moon’s soil could hold a lander before Apollo landed.
  • Spirit and Opportunity found evidence that water once shaped Mars.
  • Ingenuity made the first powered flight on another planet.

Why it matters:
These machines are the foundation of today’s exploration. Giving them a voice builds a personal connection and inspires the next generation of scientists and engineers.

What it does:

  • A landing page with a looping galaxy video.
  • A 12-scene story mode with recorded narration.
  • An interactive Moon and Mars map of left-behind hardware.
  • A scroll-driven timeline from 1967 to 2021.
  • A 13-mission archive with Moon, Mars, and deep space filters.
  • A quiz for each mission.

How it works:
It’s one static HTML file with plain JavaScript. Missions, scenes, and map pins are data lists that the page turns into the interface. Map dots are placed at real latitude and longitude. Each scene plays its own audio file. If an online NASA image fails to load, the page draws its own illustration of the machine instead. It runs on any web host, with no server or build step.

Benefits:
Free and open to everyone, works on phones, usable by keyboard, respects “reduce motion” settings, has reading levels for different ages, and links its facts to NASA sources.

What we hope to achieve:
Make forgotten robotic explorers feel personal, give teachers a ready classroom resource, and inspire curiosity about the science these machines made possible.

Tools and technologies:

  • Languages and web features: HTML5, CSS3, vanilla JavaScript (ES6), HTML Canvas, and HTML audio and video.
  • Fonts: Orbitron, IBM Plex Mono, and Space Grotesk, from Google Fonts.
  • Narration: ElevenLabs voice.
  • Media processing: FFmpeg for audio and video, Python with Pillow for images.
  • Testing: Playwright with Chromium.
  • Hosting: GitHub and GoDaddy.
  • Sources: NASA Science, NSSDCA, the Apollo Lunar Surface Journal, and the NASA Image Library.
  • Development help: Claude, Anthropic’s AI assistant. Check your hackathon’s rules on disclosing AI use, and describe your own role honestly.
  • Hardware: A standard laptop, with no special equipment.
